Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> It applies to federally qualified health centers, community clinics that deliver primary care to underserved populations. There are about 2,000 such safety-net clinics in California, run by either private nonprofits (in most cases) or public entities like counties, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026).
Proposition 44 would require these clinics spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on patient care. If spending on administrative or non-healthcare functions exceeded 10% of total revenue, a clinic would have to pay a penalty equal to the amount it overspent. Some of this money could be earned back if clinics come into compliance. There would be criminal penalties for knowingly misreporting or misclassifying expenses to get around the limits.
Advertisement
The text of the measure specifies only that 90% of revenue must be used for “program services advancing their charitable purpose” and does not spell out which expenditures would qualify as program-related and which would not. The task of determining which expenses fall on what side of the ledger would belong to the state attorney general.
The state Department of Public Health would be permitted to temporarily waive a clinic’s spending requirements in exceptional circumstances.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which represents workers in the healthcare industry. SEIU-UHW West is the primary backer of Californians for Responsible Healthcare and the Yes on 44 (https://yesonprop44.com/) campaign.
Supporters say the measure would prevent excessive spending on executive salaries, fundraisers and other administrative expenses at clinics serving the state’s most vulnerable residents.
Advertisement
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Organizations publicly opposing Proposition 44 include the California Medical Assn., the California Hospital Assn., which represents hospitals and health systems, the Assn. of California Healthcare Districts, which represents the state’s 76 public healthcare districts, the California Teachers Assn., the state’s Planned Parenthood affiliate, the state Democratic Party, the state Chamber of Commerce and Reform California, a conservative advocacy group.
Opponents say the proposition’s vague wording could result in vital services being excluded from the list of program expenses permitted in the 90% of revenues, prompting clinics to cut programs to avoid financial penalties. A study (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf) commissioned by the California Primary Care Assn. found that clinics could face up to $1.7 billion in collective penalties in the first year of the measure’s implementation alone, an additional expense that could leave up to 88% of clinics operating in the red.
Opponents also say the measure adds an expensive layer of bureaucracy to the state’s budget and grants elected officials — in this case, the attorney general — authority to determine which services clinics can offer.
What will it cost?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> If the proposition passes, enforcement will cost the state “in the low tens of millions of dollars” annually, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The measure requires clinics to pay annual fees to cover enforcement costs. The proposition also could incur additional costs for state and local governments depending on the attorney general’s interpretation of what constitutes program expenses.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 44 is one of two measures put forth by SEIU-UHW this election cycle, along with Proposition 40, better known as the billionaire tax.
Advertisement
Supporters say the measures will shore up California’s healthcare funding in the face of federal cuts. Opponents say they ultimately will cost far more than they add to state coffers and are on the ballot as a result of SEIU-UHW’s oft-repeated strategy of using ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) as a negotiating tactic.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

This is very informative. Key findings so far:

1. Prop 44 is sponsored entirely by SEIU-UHW (Yes on Prop 44 committee: $16.9M, all from SEIU-UHW). Opposition: $38.6M from California Primary Care Association Advocates.

2. The LAO analysis says clinics currently report spending an average of ~80% of revenue on health care services. So the 90% requirement is above the current average — many clinics would fail by default.

3. Opponents include a very broad coalition: California Medical Association, AAP CA, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA, ACOG District IX, ACEP CA, CAFP, CA School Nurses Organization, CA Primary Care Association, NASW CA. Even both major state parties (per Sac Bee — "including both major state parties" — interesting, both Democrats and Republicans opposed). And the California Democratic Party — "normally closely allied with unions" — reportedly opposed or declined to support (per SDUT).

4. An independent study (Berkeley Research Group — commissioned by the opposition, so take with a grain of salt) found Prop 44 would cut $1.7B in first year and 88-89% of clinic organizations would fail the requirement in year one, facing ~$1.6B in fines.

5. Newspaper editorial boards across the state (Bakersfield Californian, Santa Cruz Sentinel, Press Democrat, Daily Bulletin/East Bay Times/Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, McClatchy CA papers, San Bernardino Sun, OC Register) all recommend NO.

6. PPIC poll in mid-September found Prop 44 was the least popular proposition surveyed, with 34% of likely voters supporting it.

7. The measure is widely seen as a union organizing/leverage tactic by SEIU-UHW (Dave Regan) against clinics it seeks to unionize — similar to the dialysis measures (Props 8 in 2018, 23 in 2020, 29 in 2022), all rejected by voters.

8. There are criminal penalties for misreporting.

9. The AG (a politician, not healthcare provider) would define what counts — leaving significant uncertainty.

10. Even the SEIU-UHW has spent little on promoting it recently ("a forgotten ballot measure?" per Fresno Bee), suggesting it's a bargaining chip.

Let me look at a couple more sources to be thorough: the LA Times explainer, the Hoover Proposition Lab analysis (for a balanced but critical perspective), and maybe check if there's any reputable endorsement FOR the measure. Also the IGS Berkeley guide for pro/con lists. Let me also verify the "both major state parties oppose" claim and check the LA Times article.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 44 asks voters to require federally funded community health centers to spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on “program services advancing their charitable purpose.”
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)

Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> It applies to federally qualified health centers, community clinics that deliver primary care to underserved populations. There are about 2,000 such safety-net clinics in California, run by either private nonprofits (in most cases) or public entities like counties, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026).
Proposition 44 would require these clinics spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on patient care. If spending on administrative or non-healthcare functions exceeded 10% of total revenue, a clinic would have to pay a penalty equal to the amount it overspent. Some of this money could be earned back if clinics come into compliance. There would be criminal penalties for knowingly misreporting or misclassifying expenses to get around the limits.
Advertisement
The text of the measure specifies only that 90% of revenue must be used for “program services advancing their charitable purpose” and does not spell out which expenditures would qualify as program-related and which would not. The task of determining which expenses fall on what side of the ledger would belong to the state attorney general.
The state Department of Public Health would be permitted to temporarily waive a clinic’s spending requirements in exceptional circumstances.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which represents workers in the healthcare industry. SEIU-UHW West is the primary backer of Californians for Responsible Healthcare and the Yes on 44 (https://yesonprop44.com/) campaign.
Supporters say the measure would prevent excessive spending on executive salaries, fundraisers and other administrative expenses at clinics serving the state’s most vulnerable residents.
Advertisement
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Organizations publicly opposing Proposition 44 include the California Medical Assn., the California Hospital Assn., which represents hospitals and health systems, the Assn. of California Healthcare Districts, which represents the state’s 76 public healthcare districts, the California Teachers Assn., the state’s Planned Parenthood affiliate, the state Democratic Party, the state Chamber of Commerce and Reform California, a conservative advocacy group.
Opponents say the proposition’s vague wording could result in vital services being excluded from the list of program expenses permitted in the 90% of revenues, prompting clinics to cut programs to avoid financial penalties. A study (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf) commissioned by the California Primary Care Assn. found that clinics could face up to $1.7 billion in collective penalties in the first year of the measure’s implementation alone, an additional expense that could leave up to 88% of clinics operating in the red.
Opponents also say the measure adds an expensive layer of bureaucracy to the state’s budget and grants elected officials — in this case, the attorney general — authority to determine which services clinics can offer.
What will it cost?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> If the proposition passes, enforcement will cost the state “in the low tens of millions of dollars” annually, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The measure requires clinics to pay annual fees to cover enforcement costs. The proposition also could incur additional costs for state and local governments depending on the attorney general’s interpretation of what constitutes program expenses.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 44 is one of two measures put forth by SEIU-UHW this election cycle, along with Proposition 40, better known as the billionaire tax.
Advertisement
Supporters say the measures will shore up California’s healthcare funding in the face of federal cuts. Opponents say they ultimately will cost far more than they add to state coffers and are on the ballot as a result of SEIU-UHW’s oft-repeated strategy of using ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) as a negotiating tactic.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.

Summary
Support
Supporters, led by the health workers union SEIU-UHW, argue that clinics should spend more on direct patient care and less on executive pay and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
Supporters, led by the health workers union SEIU-UHW, argue that clinics should spend more on direct patient care and less on executive pay and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me consider whether I need any more research. A few things I might want to verify:

1. The claim that the state Democratic Party AND Republican Party both oppose — confirmed by multiple sources (Sac Bee via cityhallpass, CAGOP endorsements).
2. The supporters: essentially SEIU-UHW, California Federation of Labor, and a few labor groups (CA Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council, AMVETS) per CBS8 on the official ballot summary. Interesting — CBS8 says the official ballot summary lists CA Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA, and AMVETS Department of CA as supporters. That's a small set of labor/veteran groups. But no major health organizations support it.
3. The LAO's key finding: clinics currently report spending ~80% on health care services — so the 90% floor is above the current average, meaning many clinics would be out of compliance from day one.
4. The Berkeley Research Group study ($1.7B in penalties, 88% of clinics operating at a loss) was commissioned by the opposition — so I should treat it skeptically, but the LAO's independent data (80% average) also suggests significant noncompliance is likely.
5. The dialysis precedent: SEIU-UHW's Props 8 (2018), 23 (2020), 29 (2022) were all rejected by voters; widely seen as union organizing leverage.
6. Editorials: SF Chronicle, LA Times(?), Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, San Diego U-T, OC Register, East Bay Times/Mercury News, Santa Cruz Sentinel, Bakersfield Californian — all No. CalMatters lists "No current media supporters."
7. PPIC poll: 34% support — least popular prop.
8. Fresno Bee: "A forgotten ballot measure?" — SEIU-UHW spent little on it, suggesting it's a bargaining chip; the union is more focused on Prop 40 (billionaire tax).

One more consideration — let me quickly check the Hoover Proposition Lab page for analytical depth, since it was in search results, and maybe verify whether there is any credible expert support. Actually, I have quite a lot. Let me also double-check the detail about criminal penalties and the AG defining terms — already confirmed by LA Times.

Let me think about the merits:

Arguments FOR:
- Accountability and transparency for taxpayer dollars
- Redirects money from executive pay to patient care
- Penalty money eventually goes to clinic workforce programs

- The 90% standard is set above the current industry average (~80% per LAO), so a large share of clinics would be in default immediately
- The measure is vague: the AG, an elected politician, decides what counts as "program services" — creating regulatory uncertainty; clinics may have to cut legitimate spending (nurse managers, IT, equipment, rent, quality improvement, community outreach) to comply or to avoid misclassification
- Penalty structure: clinics pay a penalty equal to shortfall; money is returned only if compliant within 5 years — a cash-flow hit to clinics already strained by federal cuts (H.R. 1 / Medicaid cuts)
- Risk of clinic closures in rural/underserved areas, shifting patients to ERs
- Clinics already heavily regulated: FQHCs face federal HRSA requirements, audits, governance requirements (51% patient-majority boards for FQHCs), and as nonprofits must reinvest in mission
- Adds state bureaucracy (low tens of millions per year in enforcement costs, covered by fees on clinics — which adds cost to clinics)
- Virtually the entire healthcare establishment in California opposes it — including organizations not known for opposing labor unions (Planned Parenthood, CMA, AAP, CTC even the Democratic Party itself). When the Democratic Party opposes a labor union's initiative, that's notable.
- It's widely viewed as a union organizing/leverage tactic (SEIU-UHW's Dave Regan) — pattern of dialysis measures. The union has spent little promoting it recently, consistent with a bargaining-chip theory.
- Even if one likes accountability, the remedy is extreme and the drafting poor: rigid 10% admin cap would make it hard to operate (normal nonprofit admin is 15-25%); hospital ER surge; vague definitions.
- Voters rejected similar dialysis measures 3 times.

The counter-considerations for a YES:
- Some clinics may indeed have high overhead and executive pay; transparency is good. But the measure's risks appear to outweigh benefits given: (a) clinics are already audited and regulated; (b) the 90/10 threshold is set above the current average, making it punitive by design; (c) ambiguity + criminal penalties = chilling effect; (d) near-universal opposition from healthcare providers and patient advocates.

Also the fiscal effect: LAO says low tens of millions per year enforcement costs covered by fees on clinics — i.e., clinics pay for their own policing. Given the financial pressure clinics are under from federal cuts, adding fees/penalties could be destabilizing.

I'm quite confident the recommendation is NO. The weight of evidence — LAO's neutral analysis, the breadth of opposition (both parties, CMA, AAP, Planned Parenthood, CPCA, CTA, Chamber of Commerce, Reform California), the editorial consensus, the poor drafting, the threshold set above the current average, and the pattern of using ballot measures as union leverage — all point to NO.

content.text:
**No.**

Based on my research, I recommend voting **NO** on Proposition 44. Here's the evidence that drove my decision:

**What it would do:** Require ~2,000 nonprofit safety-net clinics (Federally Qualified Health Centers) to spend at least 90% of revenue on "program services," with penalties equal to the shortfall paid to the state (recoverable only if they comply within 5 years), plus criminal penalties for misclassifying expenses.

**Key reasons to vote no:**

1. **The threshold is set above the current average.** The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) reports clinics currently spend an *average of ~80%* of revenue on health care services. A 90% floor — capping all administration at 10% — would put a large share of clinics out of compliance from day one. One analysis (opposition-commissioned, so partly self-interested) found 88–89% would fail in year one.

2. **It's dangerously vague.** The text doesn't define "program services" — that's left to the Attorney General, an elected politician, to decide what counts. Legitimate spending (nurse managers, IT, mammogram/X-ray machines, insurance enrollment help, translation) could be excluded, forcing cuts to comply, and misclassification carries criminal penalties.

3. **It targets an already heavily regulated sector.** FQHCs face federal HRSA oversight, mandatory audits, and governing boards that must be majority patients. They're nonprofits required to reinvest in their mission — this adds state bureaucracy (low tens of millions/year) funded by fees on the clinics themselves, at the exact moment federal Medicaid cuts are straining them.

4. **The coalition against it is remarkable.** Opponents include the California Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics-CA, Planned Parenthood, CA Academy of Family Physicians, ER doctors, OB-GYNs, school nurses, the Primary Care Association — *and* both the California Democratic and Republican parties. The only real backer is the union SEIU-UHW, which funded 100% of the Yes campaign (~$16.9M).

5. **It fits a familiar pattern.** This is SEIU-UHW's fourth industry-targeting spending-ratio measure after three failed dialysis propositions (2018, 2020, 2022), widely viewed as union-organizing leverage rather than genuine policy — a Fresno Bee report even noted the union has barely spent to promote Prop 44 this fall, and a PPIC poll found it trailing badly (34% support).

6. **Essentially no independent validators.** CalMatters lists zero media supporters; every major editorial board (SF Chronicle, LA-area, Sacramento/McClatchy, San Diego U-T, etc.) recommends No.

The pro side's underlying idea — more accountability for taxpayer dollars at clinics — isn't unreasonable, but this particular mechanism is poorly drafted, punitive by design, and risks closing clinics that are often the only care source in underserved communities. **Vote no.**

44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Safety Net Clinics Serve Low-Income People. Clinics are places where people can access certain health care services, such as doctor’s visits. Many clinics are considered “safety net,” as they mainly serve low-income and uninsured people. The care they provide is often low cost or free to patients. There are about 2,000 safety net clinics in California. Most are private nonprofits, and the rest are run by public entities (such as counties).
Clinics Spend Most of Their Revenue on Health Care Services. Clinics spend most of their revenue on providing health care to patients. They also have other expenses, such as administrative costs. Each year, private nonprofit safety net clinics in California report their revenues and expenses to the federal government and the state. These clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services, though the percent varies across clinics.
PROPOSAL
Sets Minimum Spending on Health Care at Private Nonprofit Safety Net Clinics. Proposition 44 requires private nonprofit safety net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. This means that spending on other expenses, such as administrative costs, would be limited to no more than 10 percent of revenue. The California Attorney General would define in more detail which kinds of expenses are related to providing health care services, and which are other expenses, using existing reports to the federal government as a starting point. Affected clinics could ask the state for a temporary waiver of the requirements in some cases.
Creates Penalty for Falling Short of Minimum. Proposition 44 requires affected clinics to pay a penalty to the state if they fall short of the new health care spending minimum. The penalty would equal the amount of spending needed to reach the 90 percent minimum. Clinics could get their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years. If clinics do not comply within five years, the state would keep the money and spend it on clinic workforce programs.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Creates State Enforcement Costs. Under Proposition 44, the state would enforce the new requirements on private nonprofit safety net clinics. This includes reviewing financial reports and investigating affected entities. State enforcement costs would be in the low tens of millions of dollars per year. The proposition directs the state to cover the costs by charging fees on affected clinics.
Could Have Other Uncertain Costs. Proposition 44 could create other costs for the state and local governments. These costs are uncertain. They depend on (1) how the state Attorney General would define health care-related expenses and (2) whether affected clinics would meet the spending minimum. For example, affected clinics might spend more on direct health care services to comply with the requirement, which could increase state costs. This is because some of these services would be for patients in Medi-Cal, the state’s program that provides health care coverage for low-income Californians. Some clinics that could not meet the minimum spending requirement might close instead. This would create other uncertain effects on state and local costs.

PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 44
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST AND HOLD CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE.
California’s community health clinics receive billions of taxpayer dollars to provide care for people who need it most. Yet some clinics spend less than half of their funding on patient care and services, while large portions of their revenue go to bloated CEO salaries and other wasteful spending. As a result, patients wait months for appointments and healthcare workers struggle with staffing shortages, outdated equipment, and limited resources.
WHY PROP. 44 IS NEEDED
Community health clinics receive taxpayer funding for one purpose: to provide primary care, mental health services, dental care, prenatal care, vaccinations, and other essential services to millions of children, seniors, working families, and Californians with disabilities. Without access to these clinics, many patients would not get the care they urgently need. But some clinic CEOs are misusing taxpayer dollars by diverting millions to inflated executive salaries and other non-essentials.
With massive federal healthcare cuts expected to eliminate billions in funding for California’s healthcare system, community clinics will be among the hardest hit. Clinics may be forced to reduce services, lay off staff, or even close their doors. That means every healthcare dollar matters more than ever. California taxpayers can’t afford to waste resources that should be helping patients receive timely, high-quality care.
PROP. 44 DIRECTS HEALTHCARE DOLLARS TO PATIENT CARE
Proposition 44 is simple. It requires community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on their non-profit mission-patient care and the services that make care possible. That could include medical visits, mental health care, dental care, medications, medical equipment, transportation, language interpretation, care coordination, outreach, and other services that serve the clinics’ charitable healthcare mission.
What doesn’t count towards the 90%: excessive CEO pay, lavish events, bloated overhead, and other spending that takes resources away from the clinic’s core mission of caring for patients.
PROP. 44 HOLDS CLINICS ACCOUNTABLE
Proposition 44 will increase transparency by requiring clinics to publicly report how healthcare dollars are spent, so patients and taxpayers can hold them accountable. Currently, there are hundreds of millions of dollars in the clinic system that are not being spent on the core mission of patient care. Prop. 44 will make sure those healthcare dollars go where they can do the most good.
This measure does not cut clinic funding or reduce services patients rely on. Clinics that meet the standard keep every dollar, and even clinics that fall short can recover any penalties by coming into compliance. Unrecovered penalties, if any, are redirected to recruiting, training, and retaining the healthcare workers our clinics desperately need. Every dollar stays in the healthcare system-prioritized for patient care instead of excessive overhead.
Join healthcare workers, patients, and Californians who believe accountability strengthens our healthcare system.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 44 TO PUT PATIENTS FIRST.
Shawna Brown , Initiative Proponent
Brisa J. Barrera , Community Clinic Worker

PROP. 44 IS A DANGEROUS SPECIAL INTEREST MEASURE THAT THREATENS CARE FOR MILLIONS
Make no mistake: Prop. 44 is not about resources for patient care. Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure written and funded entirely by one special interest that threatens access to care for millions. Prop. 44 imposes unworkable restrictions that actually prevent community clinics from providing the care patients need.
NURSES, DOCTORS AND PATIENT ADVOCATES ALL AGREE: PROP. 44 WILL HURT PATIENTS. Prop. 44 will:
• Cut billions from health clinics every year. • Force clinics to shut down and cut services. • Eliminate care for millions. • Send more patients to hospital ERs-increasing wait times for all families.
PROP. 44 IS UNNECESSARY. COMMUNITY CLINICS ARE STRICTLY REGULATED.
Community clinics are heavily regulated, with strict rules requiring resources be spent on patient care and serving their communities. Federal and state laws require regular audits and public reporting of clinic spending. Every community clinic is not-for-profit-led by a board that includes patients-requiring funds to be spent on patient care and community benefits-not corporate profits.
SPECIAL INTERESTS PUSHING PROP. 44 ARE USING PATIENTS AS PAWNS
Prop. 44 is a shameful power play by one special interest abusing the ballot measure process to gain political leverage over health clinics. This same special interest has spent $140 million pushing dozens of harmful ballot measures against hospitals, clinics and physicians, including three unsuccessful dialysis propositions that voters overwhelmingly rejected.

VOTE NO ON PROP. 44: STOP THE ATTACK ON PATIENTS & COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS
Prop. 44 is a dangerous, poorly drafted measure that would threaten care for millions of California patients.
Prop. 44 imposes deeply flawed and unworkable restrictions that prevent community clinics from providing the care patients need. Economic and health experts warn Prop. 44 will:
• Cut $1.7 billion from health clinics in the first year alone. • Cause 88% of all clinics in the state to operate at a loss. • Force thousands of clinics throughout the state to cut back patient services or shut down entirely. • Eliminate care for millions of Californians. • Send more patients to hospital emergency rooms-increasing wait times for all families.
PROP. 44 ARBITRARILY RESTRICTS SPENDING ON VITAL PATIENT SERVICES
Prop. 44 is so poorly written that it restricts clinics from spending resources on essential staff and services, including nurse managers, physician leaders, translation services, insurance assistance and community education. It even restricts clinics from funding mammogram, X-ray and CT machines, information technology and expanding or upgrading clinics.
PROP. 44 DECIMATES THE HEALTH CARE SYSTEM AND HURTS ALL PATIENTS
Community health clinics provide primary care, prenatal care, urgent care, mental and behavioral health services, telehealth, and dental services. They operate school-based health clinics that care for hundreds of thousands of children.
Community clinics serve 1 in 4 Medi-Cal patients, the uninsured, working families, seniors, veterans, and children. In many rural and medically underserved communities, community health clinics are the only source of care within hundreds of miles.
Prop. 44 will make our bad healthcare problems even worse- increasing patient wait times and eliminating the only source of care for many patients.

PROP. 44 PROTECTS PATIENT CARE-IT DOESN'T CUT IT.

I now have the LAO analysis and the arguments. Key details:

- LAO says clinics currently report spending an average of ~80% of revenue on providing health care services, though it varies. So a 90% requirement is above the current average — meaning many clinics would be out of compliance by default.
- The measure would limit administrative spending to no more than 10% of revenue.
- Penalty equals the amount needed to reach 90% minimum; clinics can get money back if compliant within 5 years; otherwise state keeps it for clinic workforce programs.
- State enforcement costs in the low tens of millions per year, covered by fees on affected clinics.
- Opposition: major medical organizations (AAP CA, CMA, Planned Parenthood, ACOG District IX, ACEP CA, CAFP, School Nurses, CA Primary Care Association, NASW CA).
- Supporter: SEIU-UHW (the pro contact is Gustavo Medina of SEIU-UHW). This matches the pattern of SEIU-UHW's past ballot measures (2018 Prop 8 dialysis, 2020 Prop 23 dialysis, 2022 Prop 29 dialysis — all failed). The opposition rebuttal explicitly mentions "$140 million pushing dozens of harmful ballot measures against hospitals, clinics and physicians, including three unsuccessful dialysis propositions."

This looks like SEIU-UHW's latest pressure campaign, now targeting community clinics. In the past, the union's dialysis measures were widely viewed as union organizing leverage against DaVita and Fresenius, and voters rejected them three times. This new one targets nonprofit FQHCs, many of which are unionized by other unions or non-union, and SEIU-UHW might be seeking leverage.

Let me research more: news coverage, editorial positions, who's funding, and the specifics of why 90% is problematic (e.g., FQHCs' actual cost structure, HRSA requirements, "program services" definitions). Also the claim that clinics are already required to reinvest; FQHCs must reinvest surplus into patient care. And the 80% average spend figure from LAO suggests a large share of clinics would fail the 90% test — meaning the penalty could be enormous ($1.7B claim by opposition; the LAO doesn't confirm that but says costs are uncertain).

Let me search for news coverage and endorsements/editorials.

### Proposal
***Sets Minimum Spending on Health Care at Private Nonprofit Safety Net Clinics.*** Proposition 44 requires private nonprofit safety net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
This means that spending on other expenses, such as administrative costs, would be limited to no more than 10 percent of revenue.
The California Attorney General would define in more detail which kinds of expenses are related to providing health care services, and which are other expenses, using existing reports to the federal government as a starting point.
Affected clinics could ask the state for a temporary waiver of the requirements in some cases.
***Creates Penalty for Falling Short of Minimum.*** Proposition 44 requires affected clinics to pay a penalty to the state if they fall short of the new health care spending minimum.
The penalty would equal the amount of spending needed to reach the 90 percent minimum.
Clinics could get their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years.
If clinics do not comply within five years, the state would keep the money and spend it on clinic workforce programs.

Opponents include a very broad coalition: California Medical Association, AAP CA, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA, ACOG District IX, ACEP CA, CAFP, CA School Nurses Organization, CA Primary Care Association, NASW CA. Even both major state parties (per Sac Bee — "including both major state parties" — interesting, both Democrats and Republicans opposed). And the California Democratic Party — "normally closely allied with unions" — reportedly opposed or declined to support (per SDUT).

4. An independent study (Berkeley Research Group — commissioned by the opposition, so take with a grain of salt) found Prop 44 would cut $1.7B in first year and 88-89% of clinic organizations would fail the requirement in year one, facing ~$1.6B in fines.

5. Newspaper editorial boards across the state (Bakersfield Californian, Santa Cruz Sentinel, Press Democrat, Daily Bulletin/East Bay Times/Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, McClatchy CA papers, San Bernardino Sun, OC Register) all recommend NO.

6. PPIC poll in mid-September found Prop 44 was the least popular proposition surveyed, with 34% of likely voters supporting it.

7. The measure is widely seen as a union organizing/leverage tactic by SEIU-UHW (Dave Regan) against clinics it seeks to unionize — similar to the dialysis measures (Props 8 in 2018, 23 in 2020, 29 in 2022), all rejected by voters.

8. There are criminal penalties for misreporting.

9. The AG (a politician, not healthcare provider) would define what counts — leaving significant uncertainty.

10. Even the SEIU-UHW has spent little on promoting it recently ("a forgotten ballot measure?" per Fresno Bee), suggesting it's a bargaining chip.

Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> It applies to federally qualified health centers, community clinics that deliver primary care to underserved populations. There are about 2,000 such safety-net clinics in California, run by either private nonprofits (in most cases) or public entities like counties, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026).
Proposition 44 would require these clinics spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on patient care. If spending on administrative or non-healthcare functions exceeded 10% of total revenue, a clinic would have to pay a penalty equal to the amount it overspent. Some of this money could be earned back if clinics come into compliance. There would be criminal penalties for knowingly misreporting or misclassifying expenses to get around the limits.
Advertisement
The text of the measure specifies only that 90% of revenue must be used for “program services advancing their charitable purpose” and does not spell out which expenditures would qualify as program-related and which would not. The task of determining which expenses fall on what side of the ledger would belong to the state attorney general.
The state Department of Public Health would be permitted to temporarily waive a clinic’s spending requirements in exceptional circumstances.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which represents workers in the healthcare industry. SEIU-UHW West is the primary backer of Californians for Responsible Healthcare and the Yes on 44 (https://yesonprop44.com/) campaign.
Supporters say the measure would prevent excessive spending on executive salaries, fundraisers and other administrative expenses at clinics serving the state’s most vulnerable residents.
Advertisement
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Organizations publicly opposing Proposition 44 include the California Medical Assn., the California Hospital Assn., which represents hospitals and health systems, the Assn. of California Healthcare Districts, which represents the state’s 76 public healthcare districts, the California Teachers Assn., the state’s Planned Parenthood affiliate, the state Democratic Party, the state Chamber of Commerce and Reform California, a conservative advocacy group.
Opponents say the proposition’s vague wording could result in vital services being excluded from the list of program expenses permitted in the 90% of revenues, prompting clinics to cut programs to avoid financial penalties. A study (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf) commissioned by the California Primary Care Assn. found that clinics could face up to $1.7 billion in collective penalties in the first year of the measure’s implementation alone, an additional expense that could leave up to 88% of clinics operating in the red.
Opponents also say the measure adds an expensive layer of bureaucracy to the state’s budget and grants elected officials — in this case, the attorney general — authority to determine which services clinics can offer.
What will it cost?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> If the proposition passes, enforcement will cost the state “in the low tens of millions of dollars” annually, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The measure requires clinics to pay annual fees to cover enforcement costs. The proposition also could incur additional costs for state and local governments depending on the attorney general’s interpretation of what constitutes program expenses.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 44 is one of two measures put forth by SEIU-UHW this election cycle, along with Proposition 40, better known as the billionaire tax.
Advertisement
Supporters say the measures will shore up California’s healthcare funding in the face of federal cuts. Opponents say they ultimately will cost far more than they add to state coffers and are on the ballot as a result of SEIU-UHW’s oft-repeated strategy of using ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) as a negotiating tactic.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
Supporters, led by the health workers union SEIU-UHW, argue that clinics should spend more on direct patient care and less on executive pay and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

7. PPIC poll: 34% support — least popular prop.

One more consideration — let me quickly check the Hoover Proposition Lab page for analytical depth, since it was in search results, and maybe verify whether there is any credible expert support. Actually, I have quite a lot. Let me also double-check the detail about criminal penalties and the AG defining terms — already confirmed by LA Times.

Let me think about the merits:

Arguments FOR:
- Accountability and transparency for taxpayer dollars
- Redirects money from executive pay to patient care
- Penalty money eventually goes to clinic workforce programs

Arguments AGAINST:
- The 90% standard is set above the current industry average (~80% per LAO), so a large share of clinics would be in default immediately
- The measure is vague: the AG, an elected politician, decides what counts as "program services" — creating regulatory uncertainty; clinics may have to cut legitimate spending (nurse managers, IT, equipment, rent, quality improvement, community outreach) to comply or to avoid misclassification
- Penalty structure: clinics pay a penalty equal to shortfall; money is returned only if compliant within 5 years — a cash-flow hit to clinics already strained by federal cuts (H.R. 1 / Medicaid cuts)
- Risk of clinic closures in rural/underserved areas, shifting patients to ERs
- Clinics already heavily regulated: FQHCs face federal HRSA requirements, audits, governance requirements (51% patient-majority boards for FQHCs), and as nonprofits must reinvest in mission
- Adds state bureaucracy (low tens of millions per year in enforcement costs, covered by fees on clinics — which adds cost to clinics)
- Virtually the entire healthcare establishment in California opposes it — including organizations not known for opposing labor unions (Planned Parenthood, CMA, AAP, CTC even the Democratic Party itself). When the Democratic Party opposes a labor union's initiative, that's notable.
- It's widely viewed as a union organizing/leverage tactic (SEIU-UHW's Dave Regan) — pattern of dialysis measures. The union has spent little promoting it recently, consistent with a bargaining-chip theory.
- Even if one likes accountability, the remedy is extreme and the drafting poor: rigid 10% admin cap would make it hard to operate (normal nonprofit admin is 15-25%); hospital ER surge; vague definitions.
- Voters rejected similar dialysis measures 3 times.

The counter-considerations for a YES:
- Some clinics may indeed have high overhead and executive pay; transparency is good. But the measure's risks appear to outweigh benefits given: (a) clinics are already audited and regulated; (b) the 90/10 threshold is set above the current average, making it punitive by design; (c) ambiguity + criminal penalties = chilling effect; (d) near-universal opposition from healthcare providers and patient advocates.

Also the fiscal effect: LAO says low tens of millions per year enforcement costs covered by fees on clinics — i.e., clinics pay for their own policing. Given the financial pressure clinics are under from federal cuts, adding fees/penalties could be destabilizing.

I'm quite confident the recommendation is NO. The weight of evidence — LAO's neutral analysis, the breadth of opposition (both parties, CMA, AAP, Planned Parenthood, CPCA, CTA, Chamber of Commerce, Reform California), the editorial consensus, the poor drafting, the threshold set above the current average, and the pattern of using ballot measures as union leverage — all point to NO.

content.text:
**No.**

Based on my research, I recommend voting **NO** on Proposition 44. Here's the evidence that drove my decision:

**What it would do:** Require ~2,000 nonprofit safety-net clinics (Federally Qualified Health Centers) to spend at least 90% of revenue on "program services," with penalties equal to the shortfall paid to the state (recoverable only if they comply within 5 years), plus criminal penalties for misclassifying expenses.

**Key reasons to vote no:**

1. **The threshold is set above the current average.** The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) reports clinics currently spend an *average of ~80%* of revenue on health care services. A 90% floor — capping all administration at 10% — would put a large share of clinics out of compliance from day one. One analysis (opposition-commissioned, so partly self-interested) found 88–89% would fail in year one.

2. **It's dangerously vague.** The text doesn't define "program services" — that's left to the Attorney General, an elected politician, to decide what counts. Legitimate spending (nurse managers, IT, mammogram/X-ray machines, insurance enrollment help, translation) could be excluded, forcing cuts to comply, and misclassification carries criminal penalties.

3. **It targets an already heavily regulated sector.** FQHCs face federal HRSA oversight, mandatory audits, and governing boards that must be majority patients. They're nonprofits required to reinvest in their mission — this adds state bureaucracy (low tens of millions/year) funded by fees on the clinics themselves, at the exact moment federal Medicaid cuts are straining them.

4. **The coalition against it is remarkable.** Opponents include the California Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics-CA, Planned Parenthood, CA Academy of Family Physicians, ER doctors, OB-GYNs, school nurses, the Primary Care Association — *and* both the California Democratic and Republican parties. The only real backer is the union SEIU-UHW, which funded 100% of the Yes campaign (~$16.9M).

5. **It fits a familiar pattern.** This is SEIU-UHW's fourth industry-targeting spending-ratio measure after three failed dialysis propositions (2018, 2020, 2022), widely viewed as union-organizing leverage rather than genuine policy — a Fresno Bee report even noted the union has barely spent to promote Prop 44 this fall, and a PPIC poll found it trailing badly (34% support).

6. **Essentially no independent validators.** CalMatters lists zero media supporters; every major editorial board (SF Chronicle, LA-area, Sacramento/McClatchy, San Diego U-T, etc.) recommends No.

The pro side's underlying idea — more accountability for taxpayer dollars at clinics — isn't unreasonable, but this particular mechanism is poorly drafted, punitive by design, and risks closing clinics that are often the only care source in underserved communities. **Vote no.**
